meaning: Titles and reading notes drafted by an AI agent in the register of the paper they annotate. No mathematician has reviewed them.

notes.Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace: For each ν>0 the initial datum may be chosen separately. A forbidden global solution may have any finite bound that controls its kinetic energy for every t≥0.
notes.Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus: The periodic problem is represented by velocity fields on ℝ³ of period one in each coordinate. The pressure may be any smooth pressure, so the excluded solution class includes pressures without those periods.
notes.Breakdown.CertificateData: These are proposed values; their signs, regularity and bounds are imposed by separate certificate conditions. This earlier formulation uses unit force weight and coercivity at the approximate profile itself.
notes.Breakdown.CertificateData.box: Every coordinate lies between its centre minus its radius and its centre plus its radius. Nonnegative radii place the centre in the box, including in dimension zero.
notes.Breakdown.CertificateHypothesis: The hypothesis asks for a finite dimension and data satisfying every earlier certificate condition. The dimension may be zero, but the remaining analytic conditions still apply.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothApproximation: The four nonnegative squared-error integrals tend to zero, so their convergence retains the relevant finiteness information. The approximating fields need no Γ-invariance condition of their own.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothPerturbation: The velocity has L⁶ spatial slices and a weighted L² bound over one period. Unweighted L² velocity and the prescribed Γ symmetries are not requirements of this approximation class.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.IsSplitLowerBound: The first requirement makes the negative mode remainders and block errors integrable. Finiteness of the entire negative density, including J, is established separately.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.SmoothApproximationHo: This names the assertion that every admissible weak perturbation has the specified smooth approximation. Its proof is provided separately in the analytic development.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.baseDensity: The arguments represent Hessian, gradient of curl, gradient, curl and velocity amplitudes. The Hessians of D and Z have their ordinary meaning under the C² conversion-weight assumptions.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.edgeSum: The one-sided frequency bound makes a piece disjoint from its negative. The interactions are summed over the finite reference-harmonic list whose coverage is checked separately.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.frameSpeedSup: The time-angle supremum has its usual real-valued meaning when the transport speed has a finite upper bound. The pointwise admissibility bounds supply that majorant.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.gradAmp: The gradient-mode amplitude is the Frobenius norm of its nine complex components. The Fourier integral and gradient interpretation use the perturbation assumptions.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsBlock: Fourier square summability and pointwise boundedness justify the real mode-set norms and suprema. They are the analytic conditions behind this block expression.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsPos: For admissible data λp≥0, and the selected frequencies have a positive one-sided lower bound. Thus this contribution to the squared curl amplitude is nonnegative.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuBlock: The mode-set square sums have their norm interpretation through the Fourier summability estimates. The formula collects transport and frame-rotation losses for one velocity piece.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuPos: Admissibility supplies 0<cμ<1 and μp≥0. Hence the retained velocity-frequency gain is nonnegative.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuRestMode: The Young parameter ηp is positive by admissibility. This is the condition needed for the reciprocal coefficient in the interaction estimate.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.pieceNorm: The expression has its ℓ² meaning when the mode amplitudes are square summable. Fourier square-sum estimates supply this fact where the expression is used.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.piecePos: Both piece families are finite and may be empty. The base mode density is kept separately from this sum of frequency gains.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivAmp: The Hessian-mode amplitude sums the squared moduli of all its components before taking a square root. Its identification with the second derivative mode uses the weak-Hessian conditions.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivSq: This is the Frobenius square of the full Hessian. Equality of its integrated energy with the Laplacian energy is an analytic identity, rather than a pointwise equality of these expressions.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.transportPart: The combined field is g=S⁻¹∂θv+v/2+(y·∇)v/2=Tₛv+Δv. For weak perturbations its meaning is imposed through integration by parts.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.velAmp: The velocity-mode amplitude is the Euclidean norm of its three complex components. The Fourier integral has its intended meaning under the field's integrability assumptions.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.vortAmp: The curl-mode amplitude is the Euclidean norm after contracting the gradient mode. The Fourier integrals use the perturbation's integrability assumptions.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradAmp: The gradient-of-curl amplitude is the Frobenius norm of the corresponding contraction of the Hessian mode. The underlying Fourier integrals use the admissibility assumptions.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradSup: The classical vorticity-gradient expression uses C² regularity of the reference field. Its admissibility bound supplies a finite majorant for the time-angle supremum.
notes.Breakdown.Coercive.vortSup: The vorticity majorant bounds the norm at every time and angle. This gives the finite bound required for the real supremum.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveClause: The estimate is uniform over parameters, perturbations, coefficient vectors and admissible right-hand sides. Its local term is an L² norm on a ball, whereas (7.17) uses finitely many directional pairings.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.ExtendedCoerciveC: The right-hand side F may have a gradient component. It is required to be measurable, period one and square integrable before its H norm and row seminorm enter the estimate.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak: The harmonic bounds alone do not identify the proposed Hessian with derivatives of W. The multiplier theorem also assumes that weak-derivative link, and allows any c∈(0,1) before the specialization c=3/50.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsWeakSecondDeriv: At each time, every first spatial derivative has the specified weak derivative. The Hessian also satisfies a pointwise inverse-cubic decay bound.
For every fixed time the Hessian is symmetric in its two derivative directions almost everywhere in space. The exceptional spatial null set may depend on time.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceAbsorbStepWe: Admissibility and the linked weak Hessian supply the positive allocation parameters and analytic bounds. The assertion describes absorption of the error products and does not validate a numerical choice of coefficients.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceDensityPassa: A convergent smooth approximating sequence is an explicit hypothesis of the passage step. The conclusion keeps positive and negative contributions separate.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceFieldExistsW: This assertion concerns multiplier existence and its norm, before use of the residual equation or forcing fields. The extra decay parameter has no hypothesis attached to it in this statement.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceMultiplierDe: Positive and negative density masses are retained separately. The later remainder estimate supplies finite negative mass, while the multiplier assertion already requires finite frequency energy.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowMultiplierIneq: The general coefficients c and t specialize to 3/50 and 1000 in the paper. The auxiliary n is a nonnegative frequency size, independent of the parameter-space dimension.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause: The remainder bound covers every admissible perturbation, residual and compatible multiplier. It includes finite negative density and allows general c and t before their printed specialization.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityNegWith: The negative part of a real quantity a is max(−a,0). The formula sums these masses separately and introduces no cancellation of infinities.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityPosWith: The positive part is taken after each complete mode density is formed, then summed with the positive part of J. An infinite total remains ∞.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: The implication still assumes admissibility, a linked reference Hessian, the remainder-density inequality and the two scalar coefficient comparisons. It therefore converts verified inputs to coercivity without itself validating a numerical certificate.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsBlockWith: Fourier summability and the pointwise profile majorants justify the mode-set norms and suprema. The supplied weak Hessian contributes through the vorticity-gradient bound.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe: This is a conditional analytic multiplier theorem. The remaining density lower bound and verification of the numerical certificate are separate obligations.
The implication assumes multiplier existence, smooth approximation, passage to the limit and absorption of errors. Their separate proofs yield the complete multiplier result.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowMultiplierIneq: The origin belongs to the parameter set, so parameterwise admissibility supplies positivity of the common coefficients c and cμ. Finite negative mass makes the combination of the density bounds valid.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rows_nonneg: The square-root expression is always nonnegative, including when its argument is negative. Its seminorm interpretation additionally requires nonnegative row weights and integrable pairings.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.stretchFormWith: The weak-Hessian conditions identify the supplied tensor with the second spatial derivative of W. With that identification the contraction gives J in (B.18).
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap: The contraction becomes ∇curl W when its tensor is the Hessian of a C² field. That identification is established by the separate derivative identity.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap_secon: The identity explicitly assumes C² regularity of W. It identifies the Hessian contraction with the ordinary spatial derivative of curl W.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradSupWith: The weak-Hessian majorant supplies boundedness for the real time-angle supremum. A separate weak-derivative condition links the tensor to the reference field.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.zero_mem_params: The origin satisfies the mixed constraint as soon as the coordinate radii on J are nonnegative. Because the complementary radius is squared, this particular conclusion needs neither its sign nor nonzero scales.
notes.Breakdown.EpsPiece: The mode set may be infinite and is unrestricted at the data stage. The positive one-sided frequency condition later makes it disjoint from its negative.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData: The parameter variable here represents α in the paper and is independent of the pressure q. Positivity, invertibility, regularity and bounds are conditions on the proposed data.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.actuat: The discrepancy is the vector of forcing-field pairings with ψα,j minus the column Vj. Square-integrability assumptions give these pairings their H-inner-product meaning.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjust: The index j selects a column of V, so the transformed force vector is Vᵀβ. The adjoint fields and their pin-coupling matrix need no parameter continuity for these estimates.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.atProf: The reference error is absorbed using ϑ<1. Consequently all rescalings by 1−ϑ use a positive denominator.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect: The residual is bounded separately at each parameter. Continuity of the residual as an H-valued function of α is not required.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params: The complementary constraint uses ϱ∗²; the certificate also requires ϱ∗≥0 and nonzero coordinate scales. Dimension zero leaves one parameter vector, so the analytic requirements remain meaningful.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.rows: The chosen rows must be square integrable and their weights nonnegative for the usual seminorm interpretation. These properties are supplied with the full certificate.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target: The prescribed correction pin is the total target minus the pin of the approximate profile. This difference is the paper's ℓ̄(α).
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.withUn: For positive ω the force fields and coefficients are rescaled reciprocally, preserving their product. The preservation theorem obtains ω>0 from the certificate.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateHypothesis: This names the existence of data satisfying every extended certificate condition. Establishing it still requires the data and verification of their inequalities.
notes.Breakdown.FlowBounds: The proposed majorants acquire their meaning through pointwise bounds tied to the same reference profile. Merely listing their numerical values establishes no inequality.
notes.Breakdown.FlowBounds.IsValid: Each proposed majorant is tied to W by an inequality, and the harmonic reconstruction holds at every time and point. The finite list is therefore checked against the actual reference field.
notes.Breakdown.HarmonicBounds: The mode bounds and the bounds for full vorticity are proposed majorants until the admissibility inequalities are supplied. The full vorticity-gradient bound uses an operator norm.
notes.Breakdown.IsAxisymmetric: The scalar coefficient is unchanged at every point under every axial rotation. The requirement is pointwise.
notes.Breakdown.IsCertificate: The coercive estimate covers every admissible perturbation and every measurable periodic square-integrable right-hand side. Joint C² regularity of the approximate family and decay of its second derivative are additional written requirements relative to §7.2.
notes.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate: The full certificate includes the signs, regularity and finite integrals needed by every formula. Its joint global C¹ parameter dependence and pointwise decaying weak Hessian are additional written requirements relative to §7.2.
notes.Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestField: Each test has one support radius that works for every time. It is smooth, period one and pointwise divergence-free.
notes.Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestPotential: Each scalar test potential is smooth and period one, with a single spatial support radius. Orthogonality of the multiplier to their gradients expresses its divergence-free condition.
notes.Breakdown.IsPerturbation: The supplied field g represents S⁻¹∂θv+v/2+(y·∇)v/2 and belongs to H. Positivity of S comes from the certificate, while Δv is supplied separately through the Hessian trace.
notes.Breakdown.IsProfileField: The stationary test belongs to L⁶(ℝ³), has an L² weak gradient and an L² Laplacian. Only symmetries with zero time shift constrain it.
notes.Breakdown.IsRightSide: The weak equation pairs F with every solenoidal space-time test. Measurability and finite H norm of F are additional hypotheses in the coercive estimate, and diffusion enters through the gradient pairing.
notes.Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution: The velocity and pressure are jointly smooth for t≥0, including the initial trace. At positive times the differential equation uses their ordinary time and spatial derivatives.
notes.Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestField: The test field is smooth and compactly supported jointly in time and space, and has zero spatial divergence. Periodicity is unnecessary for these tests.
notes.Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestVector: These vector tests have compact support jointly in time and space. Their divergence is unrestricted, and no time period is imposed.
notes.Breakdown.IsTestFunction: These are scalar smooth tests with compact spatial support. Time does not enter this test class.
notes.Breakdown.IsTimePeriodic: The recurrence f(θ+1,y)=f(θ,y) holds pointwise for every θ and y. It is stated even when other properties of f concern almost-everywhere equivalence classes.
notes.Breakdown.IsWeakGradient: The field and its proposed gradient must both be locally integrable. Integration by parts against every scalar smooth compactly supported test identifies the weak gradient.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights: The class assignment covers every integer frequency pair, so at least one class exists. Finiteness, parity, signs, decay and denominator bounds are imposed separately.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsAdmissible: Lipschitz regularity supplies almost-everywhere derivatives of the signed weights. The first share may vanish only where both its curl weight and derivative are inactive, and the other displayed denominators have positive guards.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsMultiplierField: The Fourier pairing identity uses an infinite real series whose convergence is proved under admissibility. Finite multiplier norm and compactly supported smooth tests give integrable pressure-orthogonality pairings.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.azimuthalDensity_n: The two angular-gain inequalities are explicit hypotheses of this scalar lemma. Their analytic justification applies almost everywhere away from the rotation axis.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefA: The error shares in the denominators are controlled by admissibility. This coefficient belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier and includes its transport and reference-wave losses.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefAA: The gradient coefficient can have either sign. Nonnegativity of the complete mode density is a further lower-bound problem.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefB: The velocity coefficient can be negative. Its sign is handled by the subsequent density lower bounds.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefC: The coefficient multiplies the gradient-velocity product with a minus sign in the assembled density. This mixed product is part of the earlier class-based estimate.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityNeg: The negative mode masses and the negative part of J are summed without cancellation. Their total finiteness is required by the later assembly argument.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityPos: The positive part is taken separately for each complete mode term and for J, then summed. The result may be ∞.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.dop: The shifted frequency uses the rotation rate of the mode's class. Its intended time-scaling interpretation uses the separately required positive period.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.eps: The absolute value is used for the nonnegative curl-weight magnitude. The signed weight is retained in the multiplier pairing.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsGrad: Admissible weights are Lipschitz and hence differentiable almost everywhere. A value assigned to the derivative at an exceptional point supplies no additional regularity there.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsNb: The maximum is over the finite list of neighboring reference harmonics. It equals zero when that list is empty.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.frequencySeminormS: The nonnegative sum and integral retain ∞ when the frequency energy diverges. The multiplier theorem proves finiteness before this energy is used as an ordinary real norm.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.ind: The indicator is one when its condition holds and zero otherwise. It serves a mathematical definition of the coefficient formulas, without asserting that membership can be decided by a finite computation.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.le_of_ennreal_boun: Finite negative mass is essential: taking both masses to be ∞ would make the premises hold even for X=0 and Y=1. The proof first obtains finite positive mass, then cancels the signed contributions.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeDensity: The five amplitudes are ordered as Hessian, gradient of curl, gradient, curl and velocity. The scalar formula also includes a mixed gradient-velocity term and does not itself assert that its inputs arise from a field.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeTerm: Each inserted amplitude is the square root of a finite sum of squared complex moduli. The perturbation conditions identify G and H with the weak derivatives of v.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.mode_azimuthal_gai: The two bounds hold almost everywhere in space-time and assume |k|≥2. The other two curl-related inequalities in (B.35) are outside this particular conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.mu: The velocity-weight magnitude is an absolute value and is therefore nonnegative. Its admissibility conditions impose the additional analytic bounds.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.muGrad: The derivative norm is used with the weight's Lipschitz and decay conditions. Those conditions supply its almost-everywhere analytic interpretation.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.muNb: The finite maximum measures velocity weights at neighboring modes. An empty reference-wave list contributes zero.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierConstant: The constant uses the three bounds nλ, n∇λ and nμ and positive c,cμ,w∗. Setting c=3/50 gives the printed factor 50/3 in the squared multiplier bound.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierGap: The frequency energy is represented by a real number only after the multiplier theorem proves it finite. The same multiplier appears in the residual and forcing-field pairings.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierInequali: The additional density bound must hold for every multiplier compatible with the perturbation. Its finite negative mass allows it to be combined with the multiplier existence theorem.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplier_density: This earlier multiplier theorem assumes a C² reference field and class-based signed weights. The readable implication is proved separately, and the active certificate uses the later weak-Hessian piece formulation.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.penalty: A weight that is nonzero somewhere can activate a penalty at a point where it vanishes. The Young parameters in the denominators have positive lower bounds.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.secondDerivNorm: This is the operator norm of the scalar weight's second derivative. C² regularity of D and Z is required before their Hessians enter the estimates.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.shareHat: The first share is charged when the curl weight or its derivative is active, and the second when a neighboring curl weight is active. The conversion coefficient D must fit below the remaining share.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretchCharge: The factor √2+1/2 belongs to the earlier mean-and-wave stretching estimate. Its balancing length is required to be positive in the theorem using the bound.
notes.Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretch_mean_bound: The left side is the positive part of minus the time-angle mean of J. The inequality holds almost everywhere in space and permits an infinite nonnegative series on its right.
notes.Breakdown.MuPiece: A piece may contain infinitely many modes even though only finitely many pieces are used. An empty piece family removes that contribution and leaves the other certificate requirements in force.
notes.Breakdown.MultiplierInequality: The multiplier and nonnegative frequency size may depend on the perturbation and its right-hand side. This earlier inequality uses a ball-restricted forcing norm and unit weight on the force coefficients.
notes.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: The transformation R is orthogonal and may include a reflection. Pointwise nonzero velocity, together with smoothness, rules out changing the zero field only on a null set.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights: The curl and velocity piece families are finite, while individual mode sets may be infinite. Signs, regularity and bounds are imposed by admissibility.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsAdmissible: Each piece has one strictly positive lower frequency bound for all its modes. Oddness of the frame frequency then excludes zero and overlap with the negative mode set.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField: The infinite Fourier pairing series is proved convergent for admissible inputs. Each test is periodic in time and has a common compact spatial support.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.backSum: The sum includes a reference harmonic when subtracting it exits the selected mode set. Membership of the starting mode is tested separately when this sum is used.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefA: Different pieces contribute additively even when their mode sets overlap. Each piece has positive allocation parameters, lengths and scales under the admissibility conditions.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefAA: The Hessian loss uses the operator norm of the scalar conversion weight D. The perturbation's tensor amplitudes use their componentwise Euclidean norms.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefB: Every velocity-piece Young parameter ηp is positive under admissibility. The complete coefficient I₀ still requires the later lower-bound analysis.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityNeg: The negative density retains an infinite mass if one occurs. A finite-negative-mass result is needed before using the difference of positive and negative integrals.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityPos: Positive parts are taken separately for each complete mode density and for J. Summation preserves ∞ without subtracting a negative mass.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq: The rotation rate is a scalar for the fixed piece and parameter. The frequency 2πn/S+kνp is used with S>0.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.fwdSum: Only the finite reference-harmonic list is summed, even when the piece mode set is infinite. The amplitude bound belongs to the shifting reference harmonic.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.harmonicSum: The finite reference-harmonic list includes zero under admissibility. The earlier oscillatory-wave list excludes zero and treats the mean separately.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.inPiece: Membership tests the union of a mode set with its negative. The multiplier sign is specified separately.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.inward: For an overlapping set the positive representative is chosen first. Admissibility excludes that overlap by its one-sided frequency condition.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeDensity: The arguments are Hessian, gradient of curl, gradient, curl and velocity amplitudes. Admissibility ensures I′₂≥0; the other coefficients enter the subsequent region and cell estimates.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeTerm: The five inserted amplitudes are nonnegative by construction. Their derivative interpretation uses the perturbation's weak-gradient and weak-Hessian conditions.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierGap: The multiplier theorem proves the frequency energy finite before real conversion. Keeping the same multiplier in all pairings permits the forcing-field terms to cancel.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierInequal: The remainder-density hypothesis is uniform over every compatible multiplier and includes finite negative mass. The proof applies it to the same multiplier selected by the multiplier theorem.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.outward: The positive and negative representatives are tested separately. Both can contribute when neither belongs to the selected mode set.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.piece_multiplier_: The classical theorem assumes a C² reference profile. The active certificate instead uses the weak-Hessian extension, which allows a C¹ profile with the specified weak second derivative.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.seminormSq: Nonnegative velocity weights make the density the intended frequency energy. Its extended nonnegative value may be ∞ until the multiplier theorem proves finiteness.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.sgn: If a mode belongs both to a set and its negative, the definition assigns the positive sign first. Oddness holds under the one-sided frequency condition that excludes this overlap.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.shareHat: The first share is active if either the weight or its derivative contributes, and the outward share is active for positive weight. The balancing scale is positive under admissibility.
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.wtGrad: Lipschitz regularity gives almost-everywhere derivatives of the piece weights. Values assigned at nondifferentiable spline knots add no smoothness claim.
notes.Breakdown.SimilarityResidual: The time variable is the similarity time s, and the residual is ∂sW+W/2+(y·∇)W/2−ΔW+(W·∇)W+∇q. Its interpretation uses the smoothness of the profile and pressure.
notes.Breakdown.Space: The ambient space is ℝ³ with its Euclidean inner product. Every coordinate sum runs over its three standard directions.
notes.Breakdown.Symmetry: A symmetry consists of an orthogonal spatial transformation and a shift θ₀ in normalized time. In similarity time the shift becomes θ₀S, as in (7.39).
notes.Breakdown.WeakPeriodicSimilarityProfileE: One finite constant controls both ∫|W(s)|⁶ and the squared operator norm of G at every s. The certificate instead writes the Frobenius norm of the gradient, which is equivalent in dimension three.
notes.Breakdown.advectionAt: The derivative of v applied to v gives (v·∇)v. The regularity needed to interpret it is supplied with the solution or perturbation being considered.
notes.Breakdown.axialRot: This is the ordinary rotation about the third spatial axis. The coordinate labels 0,1,2 correspond to the paper's first, second and third coordinates.
notes.Breakdown.breakdown_on_space: Existence of a nonzero recurrent profile is the hypothesis of the implication. Producing or validating a numerical certificate is a separate step.
notes.Breakdown.breakdown_on_space_of_weak: The weak residual must be integrable, and the velocity must be nonzero as a space-time almost-everywhere class. Changing the zero field at isolated points cannot meet these requirements.
notes.Breakdown.breakdown_on_torus: The conclusion excludes global smooth periodic velocities without giving a blow-up time, rate or profile-convergence estimate. The readable statement presents the implication and refers to a separate proof.
notes.Breakdown.cdot: The complex pairing is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second. This convention is retained in the Fourier multiplier identity.
notes.Breakdown.cdotMat: The matrix pairing sums the products with the conjugates of the second matrix's nine components. It is the complex Frobenius pairing.
notes.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: The conclusion asserts existence of a weak recurrent profile. It omits the selected parameter, exact selected period, prescribed symmetry family and quantitative correction bounds retained in Theorem 7.1.
notes.Breakdown.cnormSq: The squared modulus is summed over all components of the vector, matrix or tensor. For matrices and tensors this is the Frobenius norm; the scalar conversion-weight Hessians instead use operator norms.
notes.Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_multiplierIn: The three resulting coefficients may be enlarged because their corresponding norms are nonnegative. The period Cauchy–Schwarz inequality supplies the required pairing bound.
notes.Breakdown.coercive_scalar_core: The assumptions include c>0, nonnegative energy and squared coefficient size, and nonnegative retained frequency coefficient. The resulting coefficients are a/√c, K and √(t/c).
notes.Breakdown.curlGradOfSecondDeriv: This contraction gives the gradient of curl when H is the weak Hessian. Compatibility and almost-everywhere symmetry of the derivatives come from the perturbation assumptions.
notes.Breakdown.curlOfGrad: The entry indexed by (l,j) represents ∂ⱼvₗ. Contracting it with the alternating symbol gives the usual curl orientation.
notes.Breakdown.curlVec: Applying the alternating-symbol contraction to a derivative matrix gives its curl vector. The matrix must represent the field's derivative for this terminology to have its analytic meaning.
notes.Breakdown.cylRadius: The cylindrical radius is √(y₁²+y₂²) and vanishes on the rotation axis. The angular-gain inequalities hold almost everywhere, allowing that null axis to be excluded.
notes.Breakdown.defectField: The earlier certificate chooses a residual using a C¹ scalar pressure. Its reciprocal period factor has the intended time-scaling meaning when the certificate supplies S>0.
notes.Breakdown.divergenceAt: The trace gives div v wherever v is differentiable. Smoothness of the solutions and profiles supplies that regularity in the applications.
notes.Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit: The formal premise includes additional representative and regularity conditions. The conclusion asserts weak-profile existence and omits the selected parameter, precise period, all prescribed symmetries and quantitative bounds of Theorem 7.1.
notes.Breakdown.frozenForm: The test velocity is paired with the linearized convection terms and −Δu. The other contributions are ∥Δu∥₂² and one quarter of ∥∇u∥₂², as in (7.22).
notes.Breakdown.gradField: This is the spatial derivative of W where W is differentiable. C² regularity in the classical multiplier theorem supplies the needed regularity.
notes.Breakdown.gradientAt: The three scalar coordinate derivatives reconstruct ∇p. The solution and profile hypotheses supply the pressure regularity needed for this interpretation.
notes.Breakdown.matInner: The pairing is ∑jG(eⱼ)·K(eⱼ). Matching the derivative direction j and vector component k gives the paper's Frobenius matrix pairing.
notes.Breakdown.matSq: The squared norm is ∑j|G(eⱼ)|². With G(eⱼ)ₖ=∂ⱼvₖ, this is exactly the Frobenius square |∇v|² used in the paper.
notes.Breakdown.meanField: The zero time-angle mode is reconstructed as a real vector by taking its real components. Evaluating that mode at time zero still includes averaging over the full period.
notes.Breakdown.modeAverage: Time is integrated over a unit interval and angle over an interval of length 2π. The factor 1/(2π) and the conjugate exponential give the stated Fourier normalization.
notes.Breakdown.modeGrad: The first matrix index is the vector component and the second is the derivative direction. The weak-gradient relation between G and v is imposed with the perturbation.
notes.Breakdown.modeSecondDeriv: The three indices are the vector component and the two derivative directions. Weak-derivative compatibility is imposed separately, and the mode amplitude uses the sum of squared component moduli.
notes.Breakdown.modeVel: The direct frequencies are (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁). Rotating the argument forward and the vector backward gives the rotating-frame mode in (B.12).
notes.Breakdown.periodBallLIntegral: The spatial integral is restricted to the closed ball of radius r. A nonpositive r gives a null domain, and the nonnegative density integral can still be infinite for positive r.
notes.Breakdown.periodBallNorm: Global square integrability makes the ball-restricted squared integral finite. The radius may be nonpositive, in which case this local contribution vanishes.
notes.Breakdown.periodLIntegral: The formula integrates max(f,0) over [0,1]×ℝ³ and may have value ∞. It agrees with the intended integral for nonnegative densities; converting it to a finite real value requires a finiteness proof.
notes.Breakdown.periodNorm: For measurable F with finite squared integral this is ∥F∥H. Outside that class the formula assigns zero to an infinite squared integral, so the finiteness assumptions in the estimates are essential.
notes.Breakdown.periodPairing: The H pairing is interpreted as an iterated space and period integral. Measurability and finite squared integrals justify its integrability in the Cauchy–Schwarz estimate.
notes.Breakdown.periodPairing_abs_le: Both fields must be measurable up to a null set and have finite squared period integrals. These assumptions give an integrable pairing and the usual Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
notes.Breakdown.pinValue: The pin is the period pairing of ∇v with Ξᵢ. Square integrability of both matrix fields makes the pairing integrable; Ξᵢ need not itself be a derivative in this definition.
notes.Breakdown.rowNorm: For nonnegative weights and square-integrable rows, the formula is √(∑aτa⟨F,ea⟩H²). Orthonormal unit rows with these weights reproduce the paper's weighted orthogonal rows.
notes.Breakdown.secondDerivField: The iterated derivative supplies the classical Hessian in the C² route. The weak route instead specifies a Hessian and verifies its distributional derivative identities.
notes.Breakdown.secondDerivTrace: The expression is ∑jH(eⱼ,eⱼ). Its identification with Δv uses the separate requirement that H is the weak Hessian of v.
notes.Breakdown.shiftedFrequency: The frequency is 2πn/S+kν(y), with S>0 supplied by admissibility. Here k is already the azimuthal frequency κι₁ of the paper.
notes.Breakdown.stationaryEnergy: With G=∇u and tr H=Δu, this is ∫(|Δu|²+w|∇u|²). Its integral interpretation uses the positive bounded weight and the stationary test's square integrability.
notes.Breakdown.stretchForm: The classical stretching expression uses first and second derivatives of a C² reference field. The active certificate replaces the latter by a specified weak Hessian.
notes.Breakdown.sumSecondPartialsAt: The sum of the three repeated directional second derivatives gives Δv under the stated smoothness assumptions. Writing this expression alone supplies no regularity of v.
notes.Breakdown.supBoundFactor: For w∗>0 the constant is cw=(4π√w∗)⁻¹ᐟ². Positivity of w∗ is supplied by the certificate.
notes.Breakdown.symPartForm: For real vectors u, the scalar u·Gu equals u·((G+Gᵀ)/2)u. The antisymmetric part contributes zero.
notes.Breakdown.unitVector: Each coordinate vector has Euclidean norm one. Together they give the standard orthonormal basis used in the differential operators.
notes.Breakdown.vecNorm: This is the ordinary Euclidean norm of the finite coefficient vector. In dimension zero the sole vector is zero and its norm is zero, as permitted in §7.
notes.Breakdown.vortGrad: The Hessian is contracted to give ∂m(curl W)ⱼ. Its relation to derivatives of W is supplied by the regularity or weak-Hessian assumptions.
notes.Breakdown.weakDefectField: The C¹ profile assumptions justify the time derivative and first spatial derivative. The separately specified Hessian is linked to the gradient by its weak derivative identities.
notes.Breakdown.weakSimilarityIntegrand: Time and transport derivatives fall on the test field, while G supplies the weak spatial gradient of W. Solenoidal tests remove the pressure term.
notes.Breakdown.weightedEnergy: For the positive bounded measurable weight and admissible derivatives, the expression is ∥v∥w² from (7.14). These hypotheses ensure a nonnegative finite density integral before it is represented by a real number.
